# Preface {.unnumbered}

## Why this book exists

I wrote this book because I kept seeing the same gap on drilling and
completions teams considering local LLMs: a general-purpose model is
fluent, but it doesn't actually know how *this* operation talks —
report shorthand, sequencing conventions, the judgment calls a
completions engineer makes without writing out the reasoning. You can
paper over that with an enormous prompt every time, or you can fine-tune
a small local model on your own operational text so it has actually
learned the domain. This book teaches the second path, end to end, in
plain Python.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA [@hu2021lora] and its
quantized successor QLoRA [@dettmers2023qlora] made this practical on
ordinary hardware — a full retrain of a foundation model is out of reach
for almost everyone; adapting a few percent of its parameters on a
consumer GPU is not. This book builds on that shift: you fine-tune a
small open-weight model, evaluate it honestly, and keep it current, all
running locally.

## What this protects

Fine-tuning on operational text raises the same stakes as any system
trained on a company's own data: what goes into the model can, in
principle, come back out of it. This book treats that as a first-class
constraint, not an afterthought — training data handling, what stays
local, and what an evaluation harness should catch before a fine-tuned
model is trusted are covered starting in Part I, not bolted on at the
end.

A fine-tuned model doesn't replace an engineer's judgment. It replaces
having to explain your operation's conventions to a generic assistant
every single time. Deciding what a result means, or whether a model's
answer is safe to act on, stays yours to make.

## Why "industrial"

A demo that fine-tunes a model on a handful of hand-picked examples is
easy to build and easy to find online. An industrial system is
different. It has to:

- Handle real, messy training data — inconsistent formatting, duplicate
  or near-duplicate reports, missing fields.
- Prove the fine-tune actually improved something, with numbers, not
  impressions.
- Never silently regress on cases the base model already got right.
- Be auditable and reproducible by someone who was not in the room when
  it was trained.

Every chapter in Part II exists because a toy fine-tuning script fails at
one of these requirements. We fix them one at a time, in the order you
would actually hit them in the field.

## How to read this book

This book borrows the practical-first, project-based spirit of *Python
Crash Course* [@matthes2023python] — small wins early, theory only when
the code in front of you needs it, a working artifact at the end of every
chapter — but assumes considerably less going in. You do not need to have
written Python before. You do not need to know what a function or a loop
is before Chapter 1; each concept is explained in plain language,
translated into terms an engineer already knows, exactly when you need it
to solve the problem in front of you.

If you've never installed Python or set up a project folder before, start
with Part 0 — it gets you to a working setup in whichever editor or
notebook tool you're most comfortable with, with no assumption that
you've done this before.

Read it in order the first time. Each chapter assumes the code from the
previous one exists and works — this is a build, not a reference manual.
After your first pass, use it as a reference: jump to the chapter that
matches the problem you currently have (Chapter 6 if your training data
is messy, Chapter 11 if you're not sure the fine-tune helped, Chapter 12
if you suspect a newer version regressed).

Type the code yourself. Do not copy-paste from the companion repository
until you have typed it once and watched it run. This is slower and it is
worth it — and if you finish this book able to say "I can build this,"
rather than "I understand the theory," it did its job.

## A note on data

Daily drilling and completions reports are typically operationally
sensitive and confidential — which is exactly why this book reuses the
same source as the author's previous book on retrieval: real, publicly
available Daily Drilling and completion reports from **Utah FORGE**, a
Department of Energy-funded enhanced geothermal system research well
(FORGE 16A(78)-32). No anonymisation was applied, because none was
needed. See `book/datasets/README.md` for the exact layout and policy.

That said, the *technique* in this book generalises directly to a
confidential archive: everything from Chapter 6 onward — data quality
gates, evaluation, drift detection — exists precisely because production
training data is messier and more sensitive than this public one. If you
point this book's code at your own organisation's reports instead, do
not commit them to a public repository, and see
[Appendix A](appendix/appendix_a_environment_setup.qmd) for a
data-handling checklist once it is written.
